title: Composite Hit-Window Economics Playbook (Aug 2026)
content:
Purpose

This note documents an exploratory workbook and recommendation playbook that quantifies combined (composite) hit-rate behavior across multiple caching windows: short-prefix cache (per-request prefix matching), session KV cache (per-user session warm-state), and a transient hot-object layer (burst TTL). The goal is to produce actionable rules-of-thumb and a small set of scenario tables that product and runtime teams can use to estimate token-level cost reduction and tail-latency tradeoffs across real workloads.

Context and why different

We already have several analyses that look at single-cache hit curves or Monte Carlo what-if matrices. This playbook focuses on the interaction effects when three cache windows operate simultaneously and when concurrency and eviction jitter matter. Key differences:
- Models composition (not just additive savings) — e.g., a request can be satisfied by the prefix layer OR the KV layer; the order, overlap, and TTL alignment produce non-linearities.
- Adds concurrency-sensitive leakage: how multi-request bursts from the same session dilute session-KV effectiveness and temporarily reduce per-session hit rates.
- Quantifies "warm-shadowing": cases where a transient hot-object layer (short TTL ~30s) reduces the benefit of aggressive prefetching and changes payback curves.

Artifact overview

Spreadsheet: composite-hitwindow-v2 (Sheet names referenced below). Rough layout:
- Sheet: assumptions — input knobs and traffic distributions
- Sheet: scenario-matrix — deterministic scenarios (grid of hit rates / TTLs) and resulting cost deltas
- Sheet: burst-sims — small discrete-event sims for concurrency effects (sampled traces)
- Sheet: payback-ratios — expected time-to-payback for prefetching and cache memory allocation
- Sheet: sensitivity-summary — tornado charts and prioritized levers

Key assumptions (default run)

- QPS: 2,500 (global, evenly distributed across regions)
- Avg tokens/request: 60 (prompt + completion units for cost calc)
- Model cost baseline: $0.00008 per token served on host (equivalent blended cost across small/large GPUs and multi-tenancy adjustments)
- Prefix cache cost per request: negligible compute but memory overhead on shared caching tier; we model the per-token marginal saving only
- KV cache memory cost: $0.20 / GB-hour (effective marginal after pooling); session KV size per active session: 20 KB default
- Hot-object layer TTL: 30s default; eviction granularity causes ~10% variance in observed TTL

Methodology summary

1) Compose hit probabilities: for a given request, P(hit_any) = 1 - P(miss_prefix) * P(miss_kv) * P(miss_hot). We model prefix and KV as correlated via session affinity factor (rho in [0,1]).
2) Convert hits to token savings: hit on prefix often saves the full prompt recomputation (approx 70% of tokens). KV hits save continuation tokens (approx 40% of tokens) — per-model profiling used to set these splits in assumptions sheet.
3) Include concurrency leakage: simulate bursts (Poisson arrivals modulated by burst multiplier) and drop effective per-session KV hit by a multiplier derived from burst-sims.
4) Convert to $ savings and subtract cache memory & prefetching costs to produce net savings.

Representative deterministic scenarios (excerpt from scenario-matrix sheet)

Columns: scenario_id | prefix_hitrate | session_kv_hitrate | hot_layer_hitrate | concurrency_multiplier | projected_savings_pct | net_monthly_savings_usd

S1 | 0.18 | 0.12 | 0.06 | 0.9 | 9.5% | $12,300
S2 | 0.30 | 0.22 | 0.10 | 0.8 | 18.6% | $24,100
S3 | 0.45 | 0.35 | 0.20 | 0.6 | 32.1% | $41,700
S4 (conservative) | 0.12 | 0.06 | 0.02 | 0.95 | 5.1% | $6,600

Notes on numbers above: these are blended across model types and region costs; net monthly savings includes memory cost for KV pools and a small prefetching budget (see payback sheet). Concurrency_multiplier <1 reduces effective session_kv_hitrate to account for intra-session contention at peak.

Burst simulations (burst-sims sheet)

- We run a simple discrete-event sim using sampled interarrival distributions derived from production traces (anonymized) for three customer archetypes: low-interaction users, chatty sessions, and automated high-frequency clients.
- Output metric: observed session_kv_hitrate and variance under different session concurrency limits.
- Example finding: for chatty sessions with >8 concurrent requests, effective session_kv_hitrate falls by ~25% vs isolated requests due to overlapping token generation and cache priming windows.

Payback heuristics (from payback-ratios sheet)

- Prefetching payback: for workloads where prefix_hitrate < 0.25 but session_kv_hitrate > 0.15, targeted prefetching (on first 2 requests of a session) typically pays back in 7–21 days depending on user churn.
- Memory allocation: allocating an extra 50 GB to the KV pool yields diminishing returns beyond 40% session coverage for the majority of our customers; expect 80–90% of incremental savings to be captured in the first 20–30 GB increment for most mid-tail workloads.

Operational recommendations (tactical)

1) Instrument a composite hit dashboard: surface prefix vs KV vs hot-layer hits per route, plus a concurrency heatmap. This is highest ROI to validate assumptions.
2) Feature-flag targeted prefetch: enable for a small cohort of chatty-session customers; measure net token delta and tail latency.
3) Implement "burst backoff" for prefetchers: if a session shows >6 concurrent outstanding requests, throttle prefetching to avoid polluting KV entries that would be overwritten.
4) TTL alignment: align hot-layer TTLs to typical inter-request gaps per-product (e.g., 10–40s windows for chat products) to maximize composite coverage.

Risks and failure modes

- Over-prefetching increases token generation and can paradoxically increase costs if session churn is high.
- Hot-layer shadowing can hide inefficiencies in prefix indexing; run ablations to ensure prefetch is actually increasing prefix hit maturity, not only short TTL hits.
- Memory waste: bursty allocation strategies without eviction tuning increase KV pool costs with low marginal benefit.

Open questions / follow-ups (short backlog)

- Q1: Can we instrument per-session prefix correlation (rho) in a privacy-preserving way to replace the heuristic? (Owner: Eng-serving-runtime)
- Q2: Validate per-model token-split assumptions (what percent of tokens saved for prefix vs KV) using per-model profiling harness. (Owner: Research/Applied-ML)
- Q3: Run an A/B with 5% of traffic using prefetch + burst backoff and compare 30-day payback. (Owner: Product-optimize / Solutions Eng)

Appendix: quick reference to sheets and cell anchors

- assumptions!A1:A20 — knobs and distro params
- scenario-matrix!A1:G120 — deterministic scenarios and cost outputs
- burst-sims!B2:F200 — sampled traces and sim outputs, includes per-archetype variance columns
- payback-ratios!A1:D40 — per-action payback days

- Keep the burst-sim code simple; we want signal not a perfect model.
